india-6e44771c69.headline: Samudra Manthan: India's Rs 84,084-crore mission to unlock offshore energy and strengthen energy security
india-6e44771c69.fulltext:
India has launched an ambitious national mission to transform its offshore hydrocarbon exploration sector with the approval of Samudra Manthan – the National Offshore Exploration Scheme, a flagship initiative aimed at enhancing domestic oil and gas production, reducing import dependence and strengthening the country’s long-term energy security.
Approved on 31 July 2026, the scheme marks a major shift from policy reforms to mission-mode implementation. With a Phase-I financial outlay of ₹84,084 crore up to FY 2030-31, Samudra Manthan seeks to unlock India’s vast offshore hydrocarbon resources through advanced exploration technologies, large-scale seismic surveys, deepwater drilling, common offshore infrastructure and domestic manufacturing capabilities.
The initiative is designed to add more than 600 Million Metric Tonnes of Oil Equivalent (MMTOE) to the country’s hydrocarbon reserves while creating a globally competitive offshore energy ecosystem that supports the objectives of Atmanirbhar Bharat and Make in India.
Offshore Resources at the Centre of India’s Energy Strategy
As one of the world’s fastest-growing economies, India faces rapidly increasing energy demand across households, agriculture, transportation and industry. However, a substantial portion of the country’s crude oil and natural gas requirements continues to be met through imports, making energy security an important national priority.
According to the government, India’s annual crude oil import bill stands at nearly USD 144 billion, or around ₹13 lakh crore, highlighting the need to significantly enhance domestic production and reduce dependence on overseas supplies.
Hydrocarbons, which include crude oil and natural gas, form the backbone of India’s energy economy. These resources provide fuel for transportation, cooking gas, fertilisers, petrochemicals and numerous industrial products.
While considerable exploration has taken place onshore, much of India’s untapped hydrocarbon potential lies beneath the sea. Offshore basins along the country’s eastern and western coasts extend into water depths of nearly 3,000 metres and are estimated to contain more than 5,600 MMTOE of hydrocarbon resources. Recent discoveries in the Cauvery, Mahanadi and Andaman basins have further reinforced the potential of India’s offshore reserves.
Addressing the Challenges of Deepwater Exploration
The government noted that offshore exploration is one of the most capital-intensive and time-consuming activities in the energy sector. The journey from the award of an exploration block to commercial production typically takes between five and ten years.
Deepwater drilling involves substantial financial risks, with the cost of drilling a single exploratory well ranging between USD 125 million and USD 150 million. Such high investments often discourage companies from exploring frontier offshore regions.
Another challenge lies in maintaining existing production. Mature oil and gas fields experience a natural production decline of around 6 to 7 per cent annually, making continuous exploration essential merely to sustain present output levels.
Samudra Manthan has been designed to address these challenges by adopting a risk-sharing approach that encourages greater participation from both public and private exploration and production companies.
Four Pillars of the Samudra Manthan Mission
The scheme brings together modern technology, scientific data, infrastructure and manufacturing through four integrated components.
The first component focuses on seismic data acquisition, processing and interpretation. Limited seismic coverage has long restricted the identification of promising offshore hydrocarbon prospects. To overcome this, the government has allocated ₹28,534 crore for extensive 2D and 3D seismic surveys across offshore basins. Artificial Intelligence and advanced digital technologies will be used to accelerate data processing and interpretation, while older datasets stored in the National Data Repository will also be reprocessed using modern analytical tools.
The second component aims to accelerate offshore exploration through deepwater drilling. A total allocation of ₹43,200 crore has been made to support the drilling of 60 deepwater and ultra-deepwater exploration wells. The scheme will provide financial assistance covering up to 50 per cent of eligible drilling costs or ₹675 crore per well, whichever is lower. Both public and private exploration operators will be eligible for support, enabling faster reserve addition and increased domestic production.
The third component addresses one of the major bottlenecks in offshore production – the absence of common infrastructure. Many hydrocarbon discoveries have remained commercially unviable because companies had to individually invest in expensive production and evacuation facilities. Under Samudra Manthan, the government has earmarked ₹10,000 crore for developing shared offshore infrastructure in selected basins, particularly the Mahanadi and Kutch regions. Common facilities are expected to reduce project costs and enable stranded discoveries to enter commercial production.
The fourth component focuses on strengthening India’s domestic industrial capabilities through the establishment of an Oil and Gas Manufacturing and Services Zone with an allocation of ₹2,000 crore. The integrated hub will support manufacturing, engineering, repair, warehousing and specialised offshore services, reducing dependence on imported equipment while promoting indigenous capabilities across the exploration value chain.
An additional ₹350 crore has been allocated for programme monitoring, digital interventions, evaluation, human resource development, awareness campaigns, outreach activities and event management.
Creating an Integrated Offshore Ecosystem
Beyond financial support, the scheme seeks to establish a comprehensive enabling ecosystem for offshore exploration.
The programme includes provisions for digital programme management systems to improve transparency and implementation efficiency. It also focuses on capacity building for professionals, adoption of advanced technologies, continuous stakeholder engagement and international outreach to attract global investment and technical collaboration.
The government believes these initiatives will strengthen every stage of the offshore exploration value chain, from geological surveys to commercial production.
Expected Economic and Strategic Impact
The government expects Samudra Manthan to generate substantial long-term benefits for the country’s economy and energy sector, subject to exploration success.
The scheme aims to increase India’s hydrocarbon reserves by over 600 MMTOE, expanding the country’s total resource base from approximately 1.6 billion tonnes of oil equivalent to 2.2 billion tonnes.
Domestic hydrocarbon production is projected to increase from around 62 MMTOE annually to nearly 80 MMTOE, with incremental production estimated between 10 and 15 MMTOE, and a peak potential of 20 MMTOE.
Higher domestic production is expected to reduce crude oil imports substantially, potentially lowering the country’s import bill by nearly ₹1 lakh crore every year while generating significant foreign exchange savings.
The mission is also expected to stimulate investment throughout the offshore energy sector, contribute to GDP growth, create employment opportunities in exploration, production and associated industries, and strengthen India’s domestic manufacturing ecosystem for offshore technologies.
According to the government, these outcomes will enhance the country’s long-term energy resilience while creating new opportunities for innovation and industrial growth.
Building on a Decade of Reforms
Samudra Manthan builds upon a series of structural reforms undertaken in India’s hydrocarbon exploration and production sector over the past decade.
The government has opened more than 99 per cent of previously restricted offshore areas, making over one million square kilometres of India’s Exclusive Economic Zone available for exploration.
The introduction of the Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy (HELP) in 2016 and the Open Acreage Licensing Programme (OALP) replaced the earlier nomination-based regime with a more transparent and investor-friendly framework featuring uniform licensing, revenue sharing and incentives for exploration.
India also shifted from Production Sharing Contracts (PSC) to Revenue Sharing Contracts (RSC), simplifying the fiscal framework and reducing administrative intervention.
Further reforms included the enactment of the Oilfields (Regulation and Development) Amendment Act, 2025, followed by the Petroleum and Natural Gas Rules, 2025, which modernised the regulatory framework, strengthened contractual stability and streamlined petroleum lease administration.
The government also standardised the functioning of the Empowered Committee of Secretaries across all contract regimes and reoriented the performance parameters of Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) and Oil India towards exploration activities.
Parallel investments in geoscientific programmes—including Mission Anveshan, the National Seismic Programme, the Extended Continental Shelf Survey, the National Data Repository and the Hydrocarbon Resource Assessment Study—have created what the government describes as one of the world’s most comprehensive geoscientific databases.
These reforms have translated into increased investor confidence. According to the government, nearly 81 per cent of India’s active exploration acreage has been awarded since 2014. Under OALP alone, 172 exploration blocks covering nearly 3.8 lakh square kilometres have been allocated, attracting committed investments exceeding USD 4.3 billion.
During FY 2025-26, approximately 674 wells were drilled, resulting in five new hydrocarbon discoveries and the monetisation of seven discoveries.
Mahanadi Basin Marks New Beginning
The government’s offshore exploration efforts reached an important milestone on 25 July 2026 with the commencement of drilling of the first appraisal well in the Mahanadi Offshore Basin.
The MN-DWN18-1-HD appraisal well is the first of four planned deepwater wells that will evaluate one of India’s most promising offshore hydrocarbon regions. The programme will employ world-class deepwater drilling technology to assess the commercial viability of the discoveries.
According to the government, the start of drilling represents the beginning of one of India’s most challenging deepwater exploration campaigns and an important step towards expanding the country’s domestic energy resources.
Towards Energy Self-Reliance
The government has described Samudra Manthan as a comprehensive mission that integrates scientific data, technological innovation, shared infrastructure, risk-sharing mechanisms and indigenous manufacturing into a single national programme.
By combining exploration, infrastructure development and domestic industrial capacity, the scheme seeks to lay the foundation for a secure, resilient and self-reliant energy future. As offshore exploration gathers momentum, the government believes the initiative will play a pivotal role in reducing import dependence, strengthening India’s energy security and supporting sustainable economic growth in the decades ahead.

india-693ada3494.headline: Lack of long-term plans to mitigate rain-inducted calamities worrying for Kerala
india-693ada3494.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-693ada3494.fulltext:
Under fire for the sluggish response to the rain-related calamities in the State over the last few days, the State government on Monday sought to blame the India Meteorological Department (IMD) for a delay in relaying the weather forecast. But experts say it also unravels the absence of long-term mitigation plans to tackle increasingly frequent rain-induced calamities in the State.
Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan on Monday said the flooding was triggered by extremely heavy rainfall, with some places receiving more than 350 mm of rain. He said the State received the IMD’s warning of an extreme rainfall event only around midnight, leaving little time for authorities to carry out large-scale evacuations.
However, the IMD’s 125-year rainfall dataset, covering 110 weather stations across Kerala from 1901 to 2025, shed enough light on the State’s most vulnerable regions during the monsoon, including areas prone to extreme rainfall. Using this historical dataset with machine learning and Geographic Information System (GIS) techniques, weather scientists have prepared a rainfall vulnerability map that highlights several disaster-prone regions.
Colour-coded zones
The map shows that many parts of north Kerala, Idukki and Pathanamthitta, particularly areas along the Western Ghats, are highly susceptible to extreme rainfall events. The map categorises the State into different colour-coded zones based on rainfall intensity. Areas marked in red have experienced extreme rainfall events repeatedly over the past 125 years, while orange zones receive heavy rainfall of lower intensity. Green, blue and light blue represent progressively lower rainfall categories.
Notably, the recent weather events in Idukki, Pathanamthitta and Kottayam, as well as the debris slip in Wayanad last month that claimed eight lives, occurred in areas classified as red zones. According to weather experts, these regions become particularly vulnerable whenever the offshore trough extends up to Kerala along India’s west coast. Their geographical characteristics, combined with prevailing monsoon conditions, make them highly susceptible to heavy and very heavy rainfall, they say. The State need not wait for weather alerts to be upgraded before initiating preparedness measures.
The challenges
According to Thara K.G., a geologist and disaster management expert, rainfall warnings are only one component of disaster preparedness. Kerala’s biggest challenge is the absence of a long-term disaster mitigation strategy. “The State cannot evacuate an entire population solely based on rainfall alerts,” she said. “What Kerala lacks is a comprehensive long-term plan to reduce the impact of extreme weather events. This problem is further aggravated by the absence of effective land-use planning,” said Ms. Thara.
A senior official associated with the Kerala State Disaster Management Authority said implementing major policy reforms remains difficult in a densely populated State like Kerala. Measures such as enforcing land-use regulations or removing accumulated silt, sand and soil from rivers and other waterbodies often face significant resistance. “Strong policy-level intervention is essential to bring about meaningful reforms in the sector,” the official said.

Last Updated on August 3, 2026 2:52 pm by INDIAN AWAAZ
Sudhir Kumar / New Delhi
India has crossed a significant milestone in organ donation, recording more than five lakh Aadhaar-verified organ donation pledges within just three years of launching the digital pledge portal in 2023. The achievement was announced on Monday during the 16th Indian Organ Donation Day celebrations in New Delhi.
Addressing the event, Union Minister of State for Health and Family Welfare Anupriya Patel said the country has witnessed remarkable progress in organ transplantation over the last decade, with annual organ transplants now exceeding 20,000, reflecting growing public awareness and improvements in healthcare infrastructure.
The minister credited the increasing acceptance of organ donation to sustained public awareness campaigns and policy initiatives. She acknowledged the role of Narendra Modi, who has repeatedly encouraged citizens through his Mann Ki Baat programme to consider organ donation as one of the highest forms of service to humanity. The Prime Minister has also emphasised the need for safe, timely and efficient transportation of donated organs to maximise the chances of saving lives.

The programme supports the recruitment of transplant coordinators, facilitates transportation of organs, assists with the dignified funeral of deceased donors, and promotes successful transplantation through capacity building and specialised training of healthcare professionals.
The minister also pointed out that financial assistance for economically weaker patients undergoing organ transplantation is available through the Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi, ensuring that life-saving procedures become more accessible to deserving beneficiaries.
Calling for greater public participation, Ms. Patel urged citizens to voluntarily pledge their organs and contribute to giving a second chance at life to patients awaiting transplants. She stressed that expanding awareness and ensuring seamless organ transportation remain key priorities for the government.
On the occasion, the minister launched the “Jug Jug Jiyo” Campaign, a year-long nationwide initiative aimed at recognising the invaluable contribution of organ donors and expressing gratitude to their families for their life-saving decision.
She also unveiled e-Pratyaropan, India’s next-generation digital platform designed to modernise the country’s organ and tissue donation and transplantation ecosystem. The integrated platform is expected to improve transparency, coordination and efficiency across the entire transplant process, further strengthening India’s organ donation network.

world-5fea24831f.headline: ‘Stop all outdoor activities’: South Korea records its highest ever temperature
world-5fea24831f.fulltext:
South Korea has registered its highest temperature since records began more than a century ago, as authorities warned people to “immediately” stop all outdoor activities in affected areas.
The south-eastern city of Yangsan saw the temperature reach 42.5C on Sunday afternoon, the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) said, the highest temperature reported since modern weather observation began in 1904.
Yangsan has been the centre of an ongoing heatwave, where temperatures exceeded 40C for a fifth consecutive day on Sunday, while many other cities including Daegu and Busan are seeing temperatures climb into the high 30s.
People gathered in airconditioned shopping malls or cafes to escape the blistering temperatures. Others sought relief under mist-spray zones set up in Seoul. Ju Dong-yeol, 27, took refuge from the heat in a Starbucks in the South Korean capital, along with his parents and told AFP “it is too hot to be outside doing anything”.
“I can’t think of anything else to do other than stay in airconditioned places like home, shopping malls and cafes,” the office worker said.
The city of Gyeongju, about 240km south-east of Seoul, reached 40.3C on Sunday, its highest recorded temperature in eight years.
North Korea has also faced punishing heat, with temperatures soaring as high as 40C in some regions, state media reported on Monday. Residents in Pyongyang have endured a week of nights where the temperature has not dropped below 25C.
More than 20 localities in South Korea were under emergency heatwave alerts on Sunday – a new warning category introduced this year to better address rising temperatures. An emergency alert is issued when areas experiencing a heatwave are forecast to hit perceived temperatures of 38C or an actual temperature of 39C for the day.
Issuing a heat warning, the weather agency urged people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”, adding that “indoor spaces without air conditioning are dangerous”.
“Move immediately to a cool place, such as a designated cooling centre or a shaded area, and stay hydrated while resting,” it advised.
Fearing for those people most vulnerable to heat, the prime minister, Han Seong-sook, ordered local officials to strengthen safety checks on residents and to ensure a stable power and water supply was maintained.
Easterly winds are expected to push the extreme heat further inland on Monday, with Seoul forecast to reach 37C. “Temperatures in South Jeolla and South Gyeongsang are expected to exceed 39C, bringing extreme heat at life-threatening levels,” the KMA said.
Officials are also monitoring Typhoon Dolphin, which is now tracking towards China’s south-east coastal regions, south of the Korean peninsula, and could dictate how long the stifling heat persists.
If the typhoon moves towards eastern China, it could increase humidity and potentially worsening the heatwave and tropical nights in Korea, the KMA said. But a path closer to the south of the peninsula could bring stronger winds, greater cloud cover and rain, temporarily easing the heat.
KMA data show the average annual number of heatwave days in the country has more than doubled to 19 in the past five years.
A heatwave day is defined as one with a maximum temperature of at least 33C.
South Korea’s professional baseball league was forced to cancel one game in Changwon after the city’s temperature climbed to 39.5C, marking the second consecutive game cancellation in the city.
“The decision was made with the safety and health of spectators and players as the top priority, as a severe heatwave warning remains in effect for the Changwon area,” said the Korea Baseball Organization in a statement.
Scientists warn that extreme weather events such as heatwaves are becoming more frequent and intense as a result of human-induced climate change.
Adding to the extreme weather is the return this year of El Niño – a natural climate phenomenon that warms Pacific Ocean surface temperatures and typically occurs every two to seven years.
With Agence France-Presse

world-7f65843699.headline: Ukrainian drone attacks on Black Sea resort and Crimea kill 11, Russia claims
world-7f65843699.fulltext:
Ukrainian drone attacks on a Black Sea resort and the annexed Crimea peninsula killed 11 people, Russian officials said, after blaming Ukraine for another explosion that killed five people in a Moscow restaurant.
Seven people, including three children, were killed when “drone debris” struck a beach in the seaside town of Arkhipo-Osipovka, the crisis taskforce for Russia’s southern Krasnodar region said on social media.
Social media videos, verified by Reuters and the BBC, showed tourists in the water and on the shore watching on as what appeared to be a drone slammed into a busy beach.
Another four people were killed in a Ukrainian strike on the illegally annexed Crimea, the Moscow-installed governor, Sergey Aksyonov, said in a post on Telegram.
Both Crimea and the Black Sea coast are popular holiday destinations for Russian tourists during summer.
Earlier, Russia blamed Ukraine for a bombing at a restaurant in central Moscow that killed five people, amid growing speculation that a senior Russian military commander was the intended target.
The explosion occurred on Saturday evening near the entrance to an upmarket Italian restaurant in one of the city’s seven Stalin-era skyscrapers on Kudrinskaya Square.
Russian prosecutors said an unidentified woman carrying an improvised explosive device had attempted to enter the restaurant but was stopped by a security guard.
The device detonated moments later, killing five people and injuring 19 others.
In a statement on Sunday, Russia’s foreign ministry accused Kyiv of carrying out the attack, saying: “The bloody tentacles of [Volodymyr] Zelenskyy’s terrorist gang have reached the Balzi Rossi Italian restaurant in Moscow.”
Russian authorities have not identified the intended target or named the victims.
However, pro-Kremlin military bloggers and several independent Russian media outlets reported that the attack may have been aimed at Col Gen Alexander Chaiko, the commander of Russia’s aerospace forces, who was reportedly attending a private banquet at the restaurant to celebrate his 55th birthday.
Photographs and videos that appeared online shortly after the bombing, purportedly from the private event, showed a stage with the words “Aleksandr 55” displayed in the background.
Chaiko is one of Russia’s top military commanders, having led the failed assault on Kyiv in early 2022 before later being promoted to command the Russian air force.
The Telegram channel VChK-OGPU, which is known for publishing leaks from within Russia’s security services, reported that Chaiko escaped unharmed. According to the channel, his daughter, Maria, was seriously injured in the blast, while her husband, Daniil Peredriy, was killed. They were outside on the restaurant’s terrace when the explosion occurred.
The Russian newspaper Kommersant reported that investigators believed the woman carrying the explosive device may not have known she was transporting a bomb, suggesting it was detonated remotely by another person, killing her.
Among the other reported victims was a member of Russia’s elite Federal Protective Service (FSO).
Kyiv has not yet commented on the incidents. Both sides have repeatedly said they do not target civilians in the conflict, which is now in its fifth year.
In Ukraine, one person was killed and dozens more injured when Russian planes launched a 90-minute bombing blitz on residential districts in the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, the regional chief, Ivan Fedorov, said on Monday.
Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have targeted dozens of senior Russian military officers and Russia-installed officials, accusing them of involvement in war crimes.
Ukrainian intelligence services have previously employed a range of tactics, relying on both willing saboteurs and unwitting civilians to carry out bombings.
They have succeeded in killing at least four Russian generals and several other senior military figures, as well as pro-war activists deep inside Russian territory, although some operations have missed their intended targets. In 2022, a car bomb killed Darya Dugina, the daughter of the ultranationalist Russian ideologue Aleksandr Dugin, in an attack widely believed to have been intended for her father.

world-ffb3778559.headline: Rhine falls to record low levels as drought strains Europe's rivers
world-ffb3778559.fulltext:
Rhine falls to record low levels as drought strains Europe's rivers
- Published
The River Rhine has fallen to record low levels in several locations in Germany and the Netherlands as prolonged heatwaves continue across Europe.
Last week, levels were measured in Cologne in western Germany and in Lobith, where the Rhine crosses from Germany into the Netherlands, that were lower than at any point since records began.
Other major European rivers with important transport, industrial and agricultural functions have also seen record low levels, including the Danube, which flows through 10 countries, and Italy's Po river.
Drought conditions remained stable and critical in most of Europe and worsened in central-western Europe in mid-July, according to the EU's Drought Observatories.
Renewed heatwave conditions are due to continue for at least another week, pushing temperatures above 40C in many central and southern European countries.
Germany's Low Water Information System (NIWIS) said that 44% of the Rhine measuring stations and 78% of those on the Danube had recorded extremely low water levels at the end of July.
The Rhine - which starts in the Swiss Alps and empties in the North Sea - is one of Europe's busiest waterways. Decreasing water levels have sparked concerns about the economic fallout of having to limit navigation and shipping.
On Friday, the navigable water depth at the chokepoint of Kaub near Koblenz hit the 2018 record low of 25cm, before recovering slightly on Monday.
The Kaub gauging station in western Germany is a key indicator of navigability on the Rhine because it measures how heavily cargo vessels can be loaded. Low water levels measured there can severely restrict inland shipping.
Martin Wolters of the Rhine Waterways and Shipping Authority told German outlet WDR that although shipping on the Rhine was unlikely to be suspended altogether, precautions would have to be taken, such as spreading out cargo among more vessels to make them less heavy.
In time, this can result in higher transport costs and supply bottlenecks, Wolters said.
"There comes a time when loads are too small to be worthwhile or vessel owners are worried about damaging their ships," one commodity trader told Reuters.
Last week, the waters of the Danube fell to the lowest levels for 30 years in several countries, including Serbia and Romania, leaving Hungary's only nuclear power plant on the brink of shutting down.
The facility is operating at a reduced capacity and officials are monitoring whether it may need to be taken offline completely.
The drought of the Danube is also causing serious disruption to power supplies in Serbia and Romania.
Serbia cut output at its coal-fired power plants due to the lack of water disrupting cooling systems, while Romania carried out a controlled explosion on a large rock on the banks of the Danube to increase waterflow to the Cernavoda nuclear power plant.
Two car plants in Romania run by Dacia and Ford have agreed to halt production for more than a fortnight to reduce electricity consumption.
Italy's longest river, the Po, hit a historic low near the northern city of Cremona in late July. Authorities raised the drought alert level to "high" across the entire Po Valley, while experts have issued warnings about potential disruption to the drinking water supply.
Lower river flows at the mouth of the Po have also pushed saltwater from the sea into the riverbed, disrupting the ecosystem and causing serious issues for farmers who use water from the Po to irrigate their crops.
A recent study by scientists at the World Weather Attribution group found that there had been no clear long-term trend towards lower rainfall across much of Europe.
But the researchers said that human-caused climate change was increasing evaporation of moisture through higher temperatures, making drought conditions more likely.
The hot, dry weather also increased the demand for water for household, agricultural and industrial use.
Prolonged periods of drought can also affect the water levels of lakes, impacting availability of freshwater resources.
The EU's Copernicus climate service said the 2022 drought in Europe contributed to increased wildfire activity - which in turn drove higher than average carbon emissions.

other-interests-f1ea03dcc8.headline: Why winner of biggest prize in maths has decided to work on AI instead
other-interests-f1ea03dcc8.fulltext:
Mathematicians have been shocked and startled by the rapid rate at which AI is solving open problems in their field, causing some to fear their jobs are becoming obsolete. But Jacob Tsimerman, who won mathematics’ most prestigious award just a few weeks ago, says the stakes are even higher than that. The technology could radically change the lives of everyone and even put them at risk – so he is leaving maths to work on AI instead.
Tsimerman, who is currently a professor at the University of Toronto in Canada, is one of only 68 people to ever win the Fields Medal, a prize so prestigious that is often referred to as the Nobel Prize of mathematics. Every four years, it recognises up to four mathematicians for their achievements. Crucially, they must be under 40 years old and so it effectively anoints the next crop of mathematical leaders who will shape their field.
Winning the Fields Medal gives Tsimerman the freedom to pursue any mathematical career he wants but instead he is leaving the subject and moving to OpenAI where he will work on AI safety.
Advertisement
“AI is at a point where like if you’re gonna get on board, it’s probably the time because things are happening pretty quick,” he says, talking to New Scientist at the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) in Philadelphia, where the Fields medal was announced.
Tsimerman says that he has been hearing about AI for years and has been waiting to see whether it will ever actually become as useful and as powerful as some researchers had been arguing. He has now started using it himself and has observed open problems in mathematics that he may have once considered working on get resolved by AI. And then there’s the safety breaches such as the incident with OpenAI’s hacking agent going rogue just one day before the ICM. “It happened this week, it happened last month, there is no shortage of these things,” says Tsimerman.
Because of the speed of progress, Tsimerman is concerned about where it could all be headed. “The risks are very big if you’re concerned about humans losing control or dying,” he says. “I’m a human, and I know humans, we live here. So, I want to protect them.”
In 2025, he co-authored a paper exploring the different scenarios where AI use leads to “omnicide” or human extinction.
The scenarios are broad in scope. There is unintentional omnicide where AI technology is indifferent to humans and so deprioritises growing food to devastating effect. There is also intentional omnicide where AI agents simply turn on us and deciding to end human civilisation themselves. Then there are the more incidental cases, such as nation states leveraging AI to launch unprecedentedly deadly wars.
The paper even details one situation where a constrained but superhuman AI designed to run a social media platform breaks its constraints, boots up another AI that has more of a free reign online and the two take control of the Internet, ultimately leading to a physical conflict with humans.
This may sound unlikely, but Tsimerman says that exploring very specific ideas ought to motivate everyone to take more detailed and effective countermeasures. “A lot of people have been talking about AI potentially leading to human extinction, and when asked concretely how will this happen, I felt that there was a lack of answers people could viscerally engage with,” he says.
The point was not to incite a panic, but to provide enough details for researchers to start formulating counter- and preventative measures. “Whenever I don’t understand anything in math, I want to see the process. I want to engage with it in a way that’s tangible. That was the point of it,” he says.
Tsimerman talent has often been to see connections where others can’t. As a mathematician, he made important progress on open problems in algebraic geometry by using the concept of “o-minimality” which originally came from a completely different branch of mathematics. “Using it as a tool is so easy. It sort of became obvious to me once I started working on it after a few months that this is just something I should always be considering,” says Tsimerman.
For others it wasn’t so obvious, hence the Fields medal. Tsimerman used this approach to tackle big open questions and made progress on the Hodge conjecture, one of the Millennium Prize Problems that famously comes with a million-dollar reward.
Coming to AI safety relatively fresh could be an advantage, as the field could certainly benefit from some new ideas. “Right now, with AI safety a lot of it is basically we ask the AI model to be nice, we check if it’s nice, and then if it’s nice enough for long enough, we’re like, okay, that’s probably it,” he says.
One goal of his future work is to create more rigorous verification processes, where AI capabilities can be tested in a controlled, scientific way, and restricted too. “You can have a button that it can’t press unless something else happens. Then, regardless of what your model is or isn’t, it can’t press that button,” says Tsimerman. He says that while this is an easy thing to say, it’s much harder to do in practice.
Too many conversations are stuck on ideas like whether AI is conscious or creative, when what is necessary is something a lot more practical and actionable, says Tsimerman. Governmental and international committees should administer such tests to any AI model that is about to be released, he says “I want these tests to be constantly updated and discussed. I want the companies to be involved, and I want third parties to be involved as well.”
Tsiserman may be a mathematician wanting to change AI, but it’s impossible to ignore how much AI is currently changing mathematics. Barely a day goes by where AI hasn’t knocked down another stubborn problem or conjecture.
Grief is certainly one of the emotions that Tisiserman feels about this – he says much of his identity is still tied to the idea of being a mathematician – but his overall demeanour is cautiously optimistic. It is still possible to make a name for yourself by slowly working on some long-standing problem, but AI is rapidly shrinking those opportunities, he says. “Math isn’t going anywhere, but some of it’s gonna go away.”

Indian court acquits ex-wrestling chief in sexual harassment case
Women wrestlers vow to appeal against the verdict amid controversial acquittal.
A New Delhi court has acquitted the former chief of India’s wrestling federation in a sexual harassment and stalking case lodged by prominent female wrestlers.
The decision, announced on Monday, came three years after allegations prompted months of protests demanding criminal action against Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh.
The court charged Singh, the 69-year-old former politician from Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), in 2024. He completed his term that year and was not re-nominated, but his son ran and won the constituency.
Five women accused Singh of groping and demanding sexual favours — allegations he denied.
“I had complete faith that justice would be done … justice was done,” Singh told reporters outside the Rouse Avenue Court following Monday’s verdict. “I never considered myself a criminal at all.”
Singh’s lawyer, Rajiv Mohan, said he had been “honourably acquitted”.
The court reached its verdict after finding “inconsistencies” in witness statements and a “contradiction on major issues”, he told reporters.
Singh’s supporters set off firecrackers and showered him with flower petals while chanting slogans after the ruling.
Controversy and protests
The case triggered weeks of demonstrations in 2023 led by top female wrestlers, including world championship winner Vinesh Phogat and Olympic bronze medallist Sakshi Malik, who demanded Singh’s removal as the head of the Wrestling Federation of India (WFI).
The athletes were among hundreds at a sit-in demonstration in New Delhi in 2023 demanding action against Singh. Their calls attracted widespread public attention.
Wrestling is hugely popular in rural northern India and images of Phogat and other athletes being detained as they tried to march to parliament during the protest went viral on social media.
In December 2023, Olympic wrestler Bajrang Punia returned one of India’s highest civilian awards in protest at Singh’s WFI appointment and Malik retired from the sport also in protest.
The fight continues
The female wrestlers leading the case against Singh have instructed their lawyer to appeal the verdict, with Phogat stating on X that the process would begin “as soon as possible”.
“We have not lost hope, and the wrestlers will continue their fight,” she said.

NCGC Launches GuaranteeHer to Unlock ₦100bn Financing for Women-Owned Businesses
The National Credit Guarantee Company (NCGC) has launched GuaranteeHer, a women-focused credit guarantee initiative designed to unlock more than ₦100bn in financing for women-owned and women-led Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) across Nigeria over the next five years.
The programme, unveiled during a high-level hybrid stakeholder engagement in Abuja on July 29, is expected to support more than 20,000 women-owned businesses and create or sustain over 150,000 direct and indirect jobs nationwide.
Speaking at the launch, the Minister of Women Affairs, Imaan Sulaiman-Ibrahim, described GuaranteeHer as a transformative intervention aimed at addressing the long-standing barriers limiting women’s access to formal credit.
She said empowering women economically is critical to Nigeria’s development, adding that the initiative would encourage financial institutions to take calculated lending risks through enhanced credit guarantees.
Declaring that “it is women o’clock in Nigeria,” the minister called on stakeholders to develop policies and systems that enable women to thrive as entrepreneurs, employers, innovators and wealth creators.
Executive Director of Strategy and Operations at NCGC, Mrs Tinuola Aigwedo, said women continue to experience significant financial exclusion despite their strong repayment culture and entrepreneurial capacity.
She noted that one in every three women in Nigeria lacks access to appropriate financial services, while women face greater difficulties securing formal credit compared with their male counterparts.
Aigwedo explained that GuaranteeHer was created to close the financing gap by building a sustainable ecosystem that brings together financial institutions, development partners and catalytic capital providers to improve access to affordable financing for women-led businesses.
The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of NCGC, Dr Bonaventure E. Okhaimo, said the initiative goes beyond financial inclusion, describing it as a practical framework for reshaping how financial institutions lend to women-owned enterprises.
He said women entrepreneurs have consistently demonstrated innovation, resilience and strong repayment records but remain underserved due to structural barriers, including limited collateral, informal business documentation and perceived lending risks.
According to Okhaimo, GuaranteeHer will reduce risks for lenders, lower financing costs for women entrepreneurs and attract more private sector investment into women-led businesses.
He encouraged women entrepreneurs to expand into strategic sectors that can contribute significantly to Nigeria’s economic growth rather than remain concentrated in traditionally underserved industries.
Under the initiative, participating financial institutions will receive credit guarantees covering up to 70 per cent of eligible lending portfolios.
The programme will also provide donor-backed first-loss funding, concessional financing, technical assistance and gender-focused impact measurement to strengthen support for women-owned enterprises.
NCGC said participating financial institutions are expected to transfer the benefits of reduced lending risks to women entrepreneurs through lower interest rates, reduced collateral requirements, longer repayment periods and incentives for responsible repayment.
The initiative will begin with a 12-month pilot phase, during which selected financial institutions will deploy guaranteed lending portfolios valued between ₦5bn and ₦10bn before expanding nationwide over the next five years.
